---
order: 9
unit: challenge
title: "Challenge: build an argument"
summary: "The course challenge, following the genre cycle. Students take a model argument apart (position, reasons, restated position), put Nib's jumbled argument back in order, choose the joining words that carry an argument from reason to reason, then build their own argument on the board and check it with a partner."
language: maths
node: [AC9E6LA03 n2, AC9E7LA03 n1, AC9E8LA03 n1]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "The position says what the writer wants, a reason backs it up with evidence, and the restated position presses the point again at the end." }
hook: "You want your school to change one thing. You get one page to convince the principal. How do you build it?"
---
An **argument** tries to convince the reader. It has three stages:

- **Position:** what you want, in one clear sentence.
- **Reasons:** each one in its own paragraph, with evidence.
- **Restated position:** the point again, so the reader leaves with it.

In this challenge you take a model apart, fix Nib's, then build your own.

## Predict: what does an argument need?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Naming an argument's stages before seeing the model makes the challenge a test of what they've learned."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You're writing to the principal to ask for more trees in the playground. Which plan will convince them best?"
  options: ["What you want, your reasons with evidence, then what you want again", "A story about a hot day, and nothing else", "Facts about trees, with no request", "Your request, said three times in a row"]
  actual: "What you want, your reasons with evidence, then what you want again: the stages of an argument. A story might help as an opening, but on its own it doesn't ask for anything."
```

## Part 1: take the model apart

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Labelling a model argument's stages is the 'deconstruction' step of the genre cycle: see the plan before using it."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#model", height: 470 }
hint: ["Click a paragraph, then choose Position, Reason or Restated position.", "Ask of each paragraph: does it say what the writer wants, give one reason with evidence, or sum up and ask again?"]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "'Our school should plant twenty more trees around the playground.' What job does this sentence do?", options: ["It gives the position", "It gives a reason", "It restates the position at the end"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "A reason says why. This says what the writer wants.", "It comes first, before any reasons."], explain: "It says what the writer wants, so it is the position." }
check: { type: board, text: "Label the position, the two reasons and the restated position.", when: "n_right = 4 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "The position comes first. Each reason has its own paragraph with evidence (hot asphalt, cooler air and calm). The last paragraph sums up the reasons and presses the request again." }
```

## Part 2: put Nib's argument in order

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Reordering Nib's jumbled argument is the joint construction step: fix a draft together before writing alone."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#order", height: 440 }
hint: ["Click a paragraph, then press Move up or Move down.", "Start with the sentence that says what Nib wants. End with the one that sums up and asks again."]
check: { type: board, text: "Put Nib's argument in order: position, the reasons, then the restated position.", when: "in_order = 1", explain: "The position tells the reader what Nib wants before any reasons arrive. Wet and scratched bikes comes before also encouraging riding, because also adds a second reason to the first. The restated position sums up both." }
```

## Part 3: carry the reader from reason to reason

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Choosing joining words inside an argument shows how the reasons are linked and how the ending follows from them."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#joins", height: 300 }
hint: ["For each gap, ask: is this the first reason, another reason, or what follows from all of them?", "Read the last sentence: is it another reason, or what the writer asks for because of the reasons?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose a joining word for each gap.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "Firstly introduces the first reason, In addition adds a second, and Therefore says the request follows from them. The joining words show the argument's plan." }
```

## Part 4: build your own

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing their own argument on the board is the independent construction step: the stages are theirs to use."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#make", height: 520 }
hint: ["Choose one change you'd like at your school. Click the first box and write your position in one sentence.", "Write two reasons, each with a piece of evidence, then a restated position. Label each part. Add a box if you need one."]
check: { type: board, text: "Write a position, at least two reasons and a restated position, and label each one.", when: "has_position = 1 and has_reason >= 2 and has_restate = 1 and n_empty = 0", explain: "Your argument has all its stages. Now check it with a partner using the checklist below." }
```

The board checks that each stage is there and labelled. With a partner, check the rest:

- Is the position one clear sentence?
- Does each reason have a piece of evidence?
- Does the restated position sum up the reasons, without adding a new one?

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Planning a real argument with the stages first is the course's transfer step."
check: { type: reflect, text: "Before writing my next argument or persuasive piece, I planned it as position, reasons with evidence, and restated position, then checked my draft against that plan." }
```

```teacher
summary: The course challenge, built on the genre teaching and learning cycle.
  Students take a model argument apart (position, reasons, restated position),
  put Nib's jumbled argument back in order, choose the joining words that carry
  an argument from reason to reason, and build their own argument on the board,
  then check it with a partner against a short checklist.
time: 55
timing: Predict 4 min · Part 1 8 min · Part 2 7 min · Part 3 6 min · Part 4 20
  min · Own writing 10 min
goals:
  - I can name the stages of an argument and what each one does.
  - I can put an argument's stages in order and link its reasons.
  - I can build my own argument with a position, reasons with evidence and a
    restated position.
struggle: "Part 4: students write reasons with no evidence ('Trees are good.
  Trees are nice.'). The checklist asks for evidence in every reason. Ask: how
  do you know? What would show the principal it's true?"
before: >
  Try Part 1 yourself, then write a quick argument in Part 4 to feel how long it
  takes.


  The challenge follows the **genre teaching and learning cycle**:
  deconstruction (Part 1, take a model apart), then Parts 2 and 3 as a
  scaffolded middle step (fixing Nib's order and choosing joining words), and
  independent construction (Part 4). On screen students work alone, so the real
  **joint construction** happens in class: build one argument together on the
  board (the class plan's opening activity) before Part 4. It brings together
  AC9E6LA03 node 2 (characteristic stages of a text type), AC9E7LA03 node 1
  (purpose drives structure) and AC9E8LA03 node 1 (structure and language serve
  the purpose).


  The argument's stages are often called thesis, arguments and reinforcement of
  thesis; the lesson says position, reasons and restated position. Claim and
  support (Patterns for ideas) is the shape of each reason paragraph, and the
  Holding writing together course's Inside a paragraph goes deeper into evidence
  and explanation.


  The board only checks that the stages are there and labelled. The quality
  (clear position, evidence, a restatement with nothing new) is judged with a
  partner or by you, with the checklist on the page. Nothing is marked by AI.
running:
  - "Predict: list the three stages on the board and keep them up for the whole
    lesson."
  - "Part 1: ask where the evidence is in each reason paragraph."
  - "Part 2: ask which word decides the order of the two reasons. (Also.)"
  - "Part 3: ask what Therefore promises the reader."
  - "Part 4: partners swap and use the checklist. One fix each before the lesson
    ends."
stuck:
  - see: A student labels the restated position as a reason.
    ask: Does it give a new reason, or sum up the ones before?
    fix: The restated position sums up and asks again. It adds nothing new.
  - see: A student's position is a question ('Should we have more trees?').
    ask: What do you want the reader to do or agree to?
    fix: "Make it a statement: 'Our school should...'"
  - see: A student's reasons have no evidence.
    ask: How do you know? What happened, or what could you measure?
    fix: "Add one fact or example to each reason: a time, a number, something
      students said."
stretch: Add a short story at the start of your argument, as in Mixing text
  types. Does it make the argument stronger? Check that it links to your
  position.
support: "A planning frame with four boxes: I want... · Reason 1 + evidence ·
  Reason 2 + evidence · So, we should..."
leads: >
  This is the end of How texts are built. The argument returns in later English
  courses on judging and persuading, and on speaking to an audience.


  Holding writing together (Inside a paragraph and Open and close) helps
  students make each reason paragraph and the restated position stronger.
exit:
  q: "An argument ends: 'Also, trees give homes to possums.' What's wrong with
    this as an ending?"
  a: It adds a new reason instead of restating the position. The ending should sum
    up the reasons and press the point again.
explain: >
  An **argument** has three stages:


  - **Position:** what you want, in one clear sentence.

  - **Reasons:** each in its own paragraph, with evidence.

  - **Restated position:** the point again, summing up the reasons.


  Joining words such as **Firstly**, **In addition** and **Therefore** carry the
  reader from one stage to the next.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: "What makes an argument convincing: the reasons, the evidence, or the order?"
    prompts:
      - Would the tree argument work with no evidence at all?
      - Would it work with the restated position first?
    notes: All three matter. Reasons give the case, evidence makes it believable,
      and the order lets the reader follow it and remember the point.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Stages on the wall
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Write Position, Reasons, Restated position on the board. As a class,
        build a spoken argument for one small change (a longer library time,
        say) and point to each stage as it is spoken.
      notes: Keep the three words up for the whole lesson.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Checklist swap
      minutes: 8
      do: >
        Partners swap Part 4 arguments and use the checklist: one clear
        position, evidence in each reason, a restatement with nothing new. Each
        writer makes one fix.
      notes: Collect a strong example of evidence to read to the class.
  questions:
    - at: end
      title: Which stage?
      type: question
      q: "'Because of this, a crossing supervisor would make mornings safer and calmer
        for everyone.' Which stage is this most likely to be?"
      options:
        - The restated position
        - The position
        - A reason
      answer: 0
      explain: It sums up (because of this) and presses the point again, so it is the
        restated position.
```

# Texts for "Challenge: build an argument" (cohesion board). An argument: position, reasons, restated position.

# region: model
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: position reason restate
role restate: Restated position
s position: Our school should plant twenty more trees around the playground.
s reason: First, trees give shade. On summer afternoons the asphalt near the canteen gets hot enough to burn bare skin, and there is almost nowhere to sit out of the sun.
s reason: Trees also make the playground a better place to be. They cool the air around them, birds nest in them, and many students say green spaces help them feel calm.
s restate: Shade, cooler air and a calmer playground: twenty trees would give us all three. We ask the school council to approve the planting this year.
# endregion

# region: order
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: position reason restate
role restate: Restated position
label: off
tools: order
s position: Our school needs a covered bike rack near the front gate.
s reason: Right now, bikes are chained to the fence, where they get wet and are sometimes scratched by passing cars.
s reason: A rack would also encourage more students to ride, which means fewer cars at drop-off.
s restate: A covered rack would protect our bikes and clear the road at the gate, so it should be built this year.
start: 3,4,1,2
# endregion

# region: joins
widget: cohesion
p: Our school should start a lunchtime chess club. [[{Firstly|However|Meanwhile}=Firstly]], chess teaches students to plan ahead. [[{In addition|For example|Instead}=In addition]], a club would give quieter students somewhere to go at lunch. [[{Therefore|But|Then}=Therefore]], we ask the principal to find a room and a teacher for Tuesdays.
# endregion

widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: position reason restate
role restate: Restated position
tools: text add
s any:
s any:
s any:
s any:
# endregion

# region: make-solution
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: position reason restate
role restate: Restated position
s position: Our school should have a water fountain on the oval.
s reason: At sport, students have to walk all the way back to the main building to fill their bottles, and some just go without.
s reason: A fountain would also save time, because classes could keep playing instead of lining up at the building.
s restate: Students would drink more and lose less time, so a fountain on the oval is worth the cost.
# endregion

widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: position reason restate
role restate: Restated position
answer: on
s position: Every classroom should have a recycling bin for paper.
s reason: Most of what goes in our classroom bins is paper, and none of it is recycled now.
s restate: A paper bin in every room is a small change that would keep most of our rubbish out of landfill.
# endregion
